extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (especially Kantian philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Kant's criteria and principles concerning physical teleology, moral teleology, and the (moral) proof of the being and attributes of God as presented in the Critique of Judgment. The page is a philosophical argument about what kinds of grounds (theoretical vs. practical) can justify theological conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical reason cannot derive Deity from physical teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of a Deity ... can never be derived from mere theoretical principles of the use of Reason (on which Physico-theology alone is based).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical Teleology, grounded in the theoretical use of Reason and empirical observation of purposive arrangements, may suggest an intelligent World-Cause but cannot produce a determinate concept of a Supreme Being or prove its reality; theoretical inquiry ascribes no more properties to objects of experience than empirical data justify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of a Deity is a priori in practical reason, not theoretical
rubrics_metrics.description: Properly speaking an Idea of a Supreme Being, which rests on a quite different use of Reason (the practical use), lies in us fundamentally _a priori_, impelling us to supplement, by the concept of a Deity, the defective representation, supplied by a physical Teleology, of the original ground of the purposes in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concept of God that can legitimately supplement teleological judgement is produced by practical (moral) Reason and is not the result of empirical or theoretical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical teleology is only propaedeutic to Theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical Teleology impels us, it is true, to seek a Theology; but it cannot produce one, however far we may investigate nature by means of experience ... Physico-theology is a misunderstood physical Teleology, only serviceable as a preparation (propaedeutic) for Theology; and it is only adequate to this design by the aid of a foreign principle on which it can rely, and not in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may use physical teleology to motivate theological inquiry, but it requires an independent (practical) principle to complete a theology; adding perfections to a Deity beyond empirical warrant is unjustified on theoretical grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealism of final causes (pantheism/Spinozism) explains away purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: This system ... does not so much resolve as explain away into nothing the question of the first ground of the purposiveness of nature; because this latter concept, bereft of all reality, must be taken for a mere misinterpretation of a universal ontological concept of a thing in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts that reduce purposiveness to mere inherence in one substance (idealism/pantheism) fail to provide a real first ground for purposiveness and thereby undermine teleological explanation rather than answering it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical grounds cannot determine a single, determinate intelligent Cause
rubrics_metrics.description: So far as we have for the basis of this concept [of Realism] only empirical principles derived from the actual purposive combination in the world, we cannot on the one hand find any remedy for the discordance that nature presents in many examples in respect of unity of purpose; and on the other hand, as to the concept of a single intelligent Cause, so far as we are authorised by mere experience, we can never draw it therefrom in a manner sufficiently determined for any serviceable Theology whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical observation can suggest multiple intelligent causes or indeterminate accounts of purposiveness, but cannot supply a determinate concept of a single omnipotent, omniscient Deity suitable for theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral teleology: final purpose is man under moral laws
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is to be in general a final purpose furnished a priori by Reason, this can be no other than man (every rational being of the world) under moral laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant treats the moral constitution of rational beings as the only a priori candidate for a final purpose; moral law gives absolute worth and grounds teleological judgement in a way physical teleology cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest good (summum bonum) combines happiness and morality
rubrics_metrics.description: The summum bonum ... consists in the combination of the greatest welfare of rational beings with the highest condition of the good in itself, i.e. in universal happiness conjoined with morality most accordant to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical Reason prescribes as a final purpose the promotion of a highest good in which happiness is harmonized with moral worth; this is the end practical reason requires us to aim at.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral proof of God: assume moral World-Cause to secure final purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequently, we must assume a moral World-Cause (an Author of the world), in order to set before ourselves a final purpose consistently with the moral law; and in so far as the latter is necessary, so far ... the former also must be necessarily assumed; i.e. we must admit that there is a God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant presents a practical (moral) argument: to make the highest good possible and to preserve the rational pursuit of that final purpose, we are justified in postulating a moral World-Cause (God). This is a postulate of practical Reason, not a theoretical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral proof does not negate moral obligation when rejected
rubrics_metrics.description: This proof ... does not say: it is as necessary to assume the Being of God as to recognise the validity of the moral law; and consequently he who cannot convince himself of the first, can judge himself free from the obligations of the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting the moral law does not logically require belief in God; the postulate of God is a practical assumption to preserve the aim of the final purpose, not a condition of moral obligation itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: final purpose and God postulate belong to practical, not theoretical, Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A final purpose is merely a concept of our practical Reason, and can be inferred from no data of experience for the theoretical judging of nature, nor can it be applied to the cognition of nature. No use of this concept is possible except its use for practical Reason according to moral laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant restricts the objective reality of the final purpose (and the resulting postulate of a moral Author) to the domain of practical reason; one should not treat these as theoretical explanatory principles in natural science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of the Supreme Cause are determined by moral teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: From the principle, thus determined, of the causality of the Original Being we must not think Him merely as Intelligence and as legislative for nature, but also as legislating supremely in a moral kingdom of purposes. In reference to the highest good ... we shall think this Original Being as all-knowing ... all-mighty ... all-good, and at the same time as just: because these two properties ... are the conditions of the causality of a supreme Cause of the world, as highest good, under moral laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To serve as a moral World-Cause adequate to the final purpose, the Supreme Being must be conceived with transcendental properties (omniscience, omnipotence, goodness/justice); these attributes are inferred from the requirements of moral teleology rather than from empirical/theoretical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human epistemic limits prevent theoretical judgment of divine final design
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience ... can never, even if we had the power of surveying empirically the whole system as far as it concerns mere nature, raise us above nature to the purpose of its existence, and so to the determinate concept of that supreme Intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant emphasizes that without omniscience we cannot judge whether nature's arrangements constitute a single final design or whether an assumed Understanding has a specific final purpose; this limits theoretical attempts to infer divine wisdom or the bestness of a plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral disposition provides subjective practical ground for belief in God
rubrics_metrics.description: He needs a moral Intelligence, in order to have a Being for the purpose of his existence, which may be ... the cause of himself and of the world. It is therefore at least possible and grounded too in our moral disposition to represent a pure moral need of the existence of a Being ... on the mere recommendation of a pure practical Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feelings such as gratitude, obedience, and humility, experienced when morally or aesthetically moved, create a subjective demand that practical reason can satisfy by postulating a moral Being; this is a non-theoretical, motivational ground for theological belief.
